lessons.title: What a letter stands for

steps.headline: The game of the hidden number

lead.text: Here is the game with the scene taken away. Someone thinks of a number and keeps it to themselves. They tell you what they did to it and what came out, and your job is to say what they started with.
Take one round. “I'm thinking of a number. I add 8 and get 14.” The 8 was put in, so you take it back out: 14 take away 8 is 6. To check, play the round forwards. 6 plus 8 is 14.
Take another. “I'm thinking of a number. I double it and get 18.” Doubling is what was done, so you undo it by halving. The number was 9, and playing it forwards, double 9 is 18.

Every round starts from a number you haven't been told. Something is done to it, and you are shown the result. You work from the result back to the hidden number by undoing what was done. Algebra is a way of writing rounds like these down, so that the writing works whichever numbers were chosen. Before the writing, there is a round for you to play.
Use the same idea on a round with new numbers. Start from the result and undo what was done.

reveal.text: You took the 5 back off the 12. The next screen writes that round down in a way that works for any numbers.

steps.headline: Giving the hidden number a name

lead.text: Writing out “my number” every time gets clumsy, so people shortened it. You may remember sums from school with a gap in them, a box where the answer goes. The round you just played looks like this:

The box means “some number”, and the sum asks which number fits. A box is awkward, though. You can't say it aloud, and a puzzle with two boxes gives you no way to tell them apart. So the gap gets a letter instead:

The letter is a name for the hidden number. It doesn't mean multiply, and it doesn't have to be x; any letter would do as well. A letter used in this way is called a variable, because in another puzzle the same letter can stand for a different number.

A line with an equals sign in the middle, like x + 5 = 12, is called an equation. The part before the equals sign is the left side and the part after it is the right side, and the equation says that the two sides come to the same number. Read it aloud as “some number, plus 5, makes 12” and you have your round again.
So far the letter has only stood for the answer. The next screen puts it to work.

Take x + 5 on its own, with no equals sign and no answer to find. What is left is a calculation with a gap in it: whatever number goes in for x, add 5. A calculation written with a letter like this is called an expression.

You can picture an expression as a machine. A number goes in at one end and the machine does what the expression says to it. A result comes out of the other end. The picture shows the machine for x + 5. Move the slider to choose what goes in.

afterFigure.text: Put in 3 and 8 comes out. Put in 10 and 15 comes out. Replacing a letter by a number in this way is called substituting, and each time you do it you learn what the expression is worth for that number.

The target beside the output is the 12 from your round. Slide the input until the machine reaches it. You found the hidden number earlier by thinking, and here the machine finds it by trial. Trial is slower, but it works for any expression. Later screens use it to test numbers.
A letter can also appear more than once in an expression. The next screen shows what the machine does then.

lead.text: A letter can appear twice in an expression. Wherever it appears it stands for the same number, so the machine puts that number into every place the letter occurs. Substitute first, then do the arithmetic.

workedSteps.text: Write 5 in place of each x.
Work out the sum.

lead.text: So far a letter has appeared on its own, or added to something. Algebra has one more habit worth learning early, because it turns up on almost every line. A number written straight in front of a letter, with nothing between them, means multiply. So 3x means 3 × x, three lots of x.
The × sign is left out because it looks too much like the letter x, and in a line of working the two are hard to tell apart. The picture shows the machine for 3x. Whatever goes in is multiplied by 3.

afterFigure.text: Put in 4 and 12 comes out, because 3 × 4 is 12. It does not come out as 34, which is what you would get by writing the 3 and the 4 side by side. When a number replaces the letter, put the multiplication sign back.

Three lots of x is also x + x + x, which fits what you saw on the last screen: x is one number, and 3x is that number three times over. Only multiplication disappears like this. In 3 + x the plus sign stays.
Next comes 3x − 4, an expression with two steps, which raises the question of which step happens first.

lead.text: The expression 3x − 4 asks for two things to be done to x: multiply it by 3, and take away 4. The order matters. Try x = 5. Multiply by 3 first and you get 15, then taking away 4 leaves 11. Take away 4 first and you get 1, then multiplying by 3 leaves 3.

Everyone needs to read a line the same way, so mathematicians agreed a rule: multiplication is done before addition or subtraction, unless brackets say otherwise. That makes 3x − 4 mean multiply first, then subtract. The same rule makes 2 + 3 × 4 equal to 14, since the 3 × 4 happens first.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows 3x − 4 as a machine with two boxes, in the order they are used. Put in 5 and 15 leaves the first box, then 11 leaves the second. You can run any expression this way: list its steps in the order the rule gives, and write down what comes out of each box.
The next question gives you a machine and a number to run it with.

lead.text: Follow the two boxes in the order the rule gives.

reveal.text: Multiply first: 3 × 6 is 18. Then subtract: 18 − 4 is 14.

lead.text: Return to x + 5 = 12. Trying numbers in the machine showed that 7 fits, and fitting has a precise meaning. Put 7 in for x and the left side comes to 7 + 5, which is 12. The right side is 12 already, so the two sides agree.

A number that makes the two sides of an equation agree is called a solution, and finding it is called solving the equation. Testing a number is a short routine. Substitute it for the letter, then work out the left side. Last, compare the result with the right side.

afterFigure.text: The picture is a balance, with the left side in one pan and the right side in the other. At x = 4 the left pan holds 9 and the right pan holds 12, so the balance tips and 4 is not a solution. Slide x along and the balance levels at only one number.
A solution has to make the sides equal exactly, and close does not count. The next screen walks through one test with some help.

lead.text: Use the routine from the last screen. The first line is done for you, and the next two are yours.

workedSteps.text: Replace x with 4.
Calculate the left side.
Compare with the right side, 9.

lead.text: The same routine with a new equation. The question asks for the left side first, and the comparison is yours to make.

reveal.text: Substitute, work out the left side, compare it with the right side. A solution has to make the two sides equal exactly, and 13 is one too many.

lead.text: A taxi charges £3 to start, then £2 for every mile. For a trip of m miles the fare, in pounds, is 3 + 2m. Read it with the rule about order in mind.

lessons.orientation: Read a letter as a number not yet given, and test whether a number solves an equation by substituting it.
lessons.nextAction: Substitute a candidate, then compare both sides.

blocks.text: Most people have played this game on a long journey. A friend says “I'm thinking of a number” and tells you only what they did to it, perhaps that they doubled it and then added something. You say what number they started with, and you are usually right, because you work backwards from what you've been told.

When you do that you are reasoning about a number you can't see, which is what algebra does in its smallest form. The letters that make algebra look so unfriendly are a way of writing the hidden number down. Once you can read them, a line of algebra reads like one of these puzzles.

This lesson starts with the game itself, played with ordinary numbers. Then the hidden number gets a name, and you build a small machine that you can put numbers into. By the end you can test whether a number you have been handed really fits.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read 3x − 4 as a calculation waiting for a number, and test whether a number solves an equation.

recap.keyIdea: A letter stands for a number. Substitute the same number for every copy of it, calculate, and if both sides of an equation agree, that number is a solution.

blocks.text: You worked back from 12 to find the hidden number in x + 5 = 12, and it was 7. You ran machines for 3x − 4 and 3 + 2m, multiplying before you added or subtracted, and you tested numbers by working out the left side and comparing it with the right. The number 3 failed in 5x − 2 = 12, because its left side came to 13.

recap.nextHook: Trying numbers finds a solution only when you happen to try the right one, and no whole number fits 5x − 2 = 12. Next you'll use a balance to find the number without guessing, and you'll see why each move is allowed.

lessons.title: Keeping the balance

lead.text: Start with scales that are level. Say the left pan holds a bag of marbles and 6 loose ones, and the right pan holds 10 marbles. Lift the 6 loose marbles out of the left pan and that pan rises, so the scales tip. Take 6 marbles out of the right pan as well and they settle level again.
Now the left pan holds only the bag, and the right pan holds the 4 marbles left over from the 10. The scales are level, so the bag weighs the same as 4 marbles. You never opened it.

The method comes down to one rule. If two amounts are equal and you take the same amount from each, what is left is still equal. The same goes for adding the same amount to each pan, or for doubling or halving both. A change to one pan alone breaks the balance, and then what you work out about the bag is wrong.
Scales are a picture of something you already know. An equation is a pair of sides that are equal, and the next screen puts the scales and the equation side by side.
Every marble weighs the same, and the scales are level. Work it out the way the scales would.

reveal.text: You took the 3 spare marbles off both pans. The next screen writes that move down.

lead.text: Now write the scales down. Call the number of marbles in the bag x. In your puzzle the left pan holds x and 3 loose marbles, and the right pan holds 11, so level scales say:

The two pans are the two sides of the equation, and the equals sign says they weigh the same. Take 3 from both sides and the left side becomes x on its own, while the right side becomes 11 − 3. That is the move you made with the marbles, and it gives x = 8.

afterFigure.text: Now see what a one-sided move does. Take 3 from the left side alone and you get x = 11. Put 11 back into the original equation and the left side comes to 14, while the right side is still 11. The balance is out, because the move changed the puzzle.
So the rule is to do the same thing to both sides. When you do, the new equation has exactly the same solution as the old one, and you can use it to simplify. The next question tests that.

lead.text: The balance shows 2x + 6 on the left and 18 on the right. You want a simpler equation with exactly the same solution.

reveal.text: Whichever move you picked, ask whether it acted on both sides. Subtracting 6 from each turns 2x + 6 = 18 into 2x = 12, with the same solution and a simpler shape.

lead.text: The scales say what you may do. To use them you need a plan for getting x on its own, and the plan is to look at what has been done to x and undo it.

If 5 has been added to a number, taking 5 away puts the number back, so adding and subtracting are opposites. Multiplying and dividing are opposites in the same way: a number trebled and then divided by 3 is the number you began with.

An opposite move is called an inverse operation. On the scales it is something you can picture. Say three identical bags balance 12 marbles. Split each pan into three equal parts, which is dividing both sides by 3. One bag then balances 4 marbles.

afterFigure.text: To get x alone, find what has been done to it and apply the inverse operation to both sides. One move is never allowed. You cannot divide by 0, because nothing undoes multiplying by 0: every number multiplied by 0 gives 0, so there is no way back to the number you started with.
The next question needs just one move.

lead.text: Four bags in one pan balance 20 marbles in the other. Decide which inverse operation gets x alone, and apply it to both sides.

reveal.text: One move was enough. The inverse of × 4 is ÷ 4, and applying it to both sides left x alone.

lead.text: Most equations ask for more than one move. Suppose four identical bags and 3 loose marbles sit in the left pan, and 19 marbles sit in the right. Written down, that is:

You can't split the left pan into four equal parts while the loose marbles are mixed in with the bags. So the loose marbles come off first, and the same number has to come off the right pan. Subtracting 3 from both sides leaves four bags balancing 16 marbles:

afterFigure.text: Now the pan can be split. Divide both sides by 4 and one bag balances 4 marbles, so x = 4. The check is the one from the first lesson: put 4 into the original equation, and the left side is 4 × 4 + 3 = 19, which matches the right side.
The next example writes the same two moves as equations, naming the opposite move at each line.

lead.text: Here the moves are written as equations. Each line names a move and shows the result, and each move is applied to both sides.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 from both sides. It undoes the + 2.
Now the × 3 has to go. Which move undoes it?
Divide both sides by 3.
Check in the original equation.

lead.text: Your turn for the last two lines.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 8 from both sides.
Divide both sides by 2. Which x makes 2x = 12 true?
Check in the original equation.

steps.headline: When the numbers go below zero

lead.text: So far every number in the equations has been positive. Equations can have minus signs and negative numbers too, and the same two ideas apply. Take 2x − 4 = −10. The 4 has been taken away from 2x, and the opposite of taking away is adding, so add 4 to both sides.

The left side becomes 2x. The right side becomes −10 + 4. To work that out, think of a temperature of 10 degrees below zero that rises by 4 degrees. It is now 6 below zero, so −10 + 4 = −6. The equation reads 2x = −6.

afterFigure.text: Dividing finishes the job. Share −6 between two and each share is −3, because a negative number divided by a positive number is negative. So x = −3. Check by putting −3 into the original: 2 × (−3) is −6, and −6 − 4 is −10, which matches the right side.
A negative answer is allowed. Nothing in the method asks for x to be positive. The last question has a minus sign and a negative right side, and the same moves solve it.

lead.text: Here 9 is taken away from 3x and the right side is negative. Decide which move undoes the minus, then check your answer in the original equation.

lessons.orientation: Justify each step of a rearrangement by naming the operation applied to both sides.
lessons.nextAction: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.

blocks.text: Picture a pair of old kitchen scales, with a pan on each side. In the left pan sits a bag of marbles, tied shut, with a few loose marbles beside it. The right pan holds a heap of marbles. The scales sit exactly level, and every marble weighs the same.

The puzzle is how many marbles the bag holds, and you aren't allowed to open it. In the last lesson you tried numbers until one fitted, which is fine for a small puzzle. The scales offer a way that needs no guessing, and it starts from a question about what you can do to them while they stay level.
This lesson follows that question. It turns the scales into an equation and finds the one rule that keeps them level. The rule then gets a hidden number on its own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll know why doing the same to both sides keeps an equation true, and use it to solve for x.

recap.keyIdea: An equation stays true when you do the same thing to both sides, so you can undo the operations on x with their inverses until x stands alone.

blocks.text: You found the bag on the scales, then did the same with letters: 3x + 2 = 23 became 3x = 21 and then x = 7. A minus sign worked the same way, and you reached x = −2 in 3x − 9 = −15 by adding 9 to both sides first.

recap.nextHook: In every example so far the moves came in an order the example gave you. Next you'll see why that order is the right one, and what to do when x has more layers around it, including a part in brackets.

lessons.title: Undoing in the right order

lead.text: Take a round of the number game with two jobs in it. “I'm thinking of a number. I treble it and then take away 9. I get 21.” The last job was taking away 9, so that comes off first: 21 plus 9 is 30. The job before it was trebling, so that comes off next: 30 divided by 3 is 10.

afterFigure.text: The picture runs the round forwards. Treble 10 to get 30, then take away 9 to get 21. The order you undo in matters. If you undo the jobs in the order they were done, dividing by 3 first and then adding 9, you reach 16. Treble 16 and take away 9 and you get 39, which isn't 21.

It is the same idea as the shoes and socks. Whatever was done last has to be undone first, and each job is undone by its opposite. Read from the result back to the start, a calculation gives you the number you began with. That is what solving an equation with several moves comes to.

lead.text: Two jobs this time. Start from the result and take the jobs off, last job first.

reveal.text: You took off the 4 first, then undid the doubling. The next screen shows how to read the order of the jobs from an equation.

steps.headline: Reading the jobs from an equation

lead.text: An equation records its jobs in shorthand. Take 2x + 5 = 11. You met the rule for reading 2x + 5 in the first lesson: multiplication comes before addition. So the left side says: start with x, double it, then add 5. The result of those jobs is 11.

afterFigure.text: Run it backwards from 11. The last job was adding 5, so take 5 away to get 6. The job before it was doubling, so halve the 6 to get 3. The machine in the picture agrees: put in 3 and 11 comes out.

On the scales those two backward steps are the two moves from the last lesson. Subtract 5 from both sides, then divide both sides by 2. The moves come in the reverse of the order of the jobs, so reading the left side tells you where to begin. The next example writes the moves out as equations.

lead.text: Read the jobs first: 5x − 3 means multiply by 5, then take away 3. The last job is taking away 3, so that comes off first.

workedSteps.text: The last job was − 3, so add 3 to both sides first.
Then undo the × 5: divide both sides by 5.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Read the jobs on x, take the last one off first, then carry on. The first line is a question about the route, and the lines after it write the route out.

workedSteps.text: Read the jobs on x in 2x + 3, then choose the route that undoes them.
Subtract 3 from both sides. It undoes the last job.
Divide both sides by 2.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Name the last job first. Then undo it on both sides, and undo the job before.

reveal.text: You undid the jobs in the opposite order to the one the expression was built in.

lead.text: In every equation so far the last job was easy to spot. Brackets can hide it. They are the curved marks around part of an expression, as in 3(x + 2), and they tell you to work out what is inside first and treat the result as one package. A number written next to a bracket means multiply, just as 3x does. So in 3(x + 2) the 2 is added to x first. The whole package is then multiplied by 3.

afterFigure.text: The jobs run in the order add 2, then multiply by 3, so multiplying by 3 is the last job. That makes it the first to undo: divide both sides by 3, which opens the package. Then take away the 2. Compare 3x + 2, where the 2 sits outside the multiplication and is added last. Brackets change which job comes last.
The same method works for any number of layers. List the jobs in the order the expression builds them, starting inside the brackets. Then take them off from the other end.

lead.text: Find the last job in 3(x + 2), take it off first, then deal with what is inside the package.

reveal.text: The 3 multiplies the whole package, so it comes off first. Then the + 2 comes off.

steps.headline: Answers that are not whole numbers

lead.text: In the first lesson you tested 3 in 5x − 2 = 12 and the left side came to 13, one too many. No whole number fits, but you can find the solution now. The last job in 5x − 2 is taking away 2, so add 2 to both sides to get 5x = 14. Then divide both sides by 5.

afterFigure.text: Fourteen divided by 5 does not come out even. It is the fraction 14/5, or 2.8 as a decimal. Check by running the machine forwards: 5 × 2.8 is 14, and 14 − 2 is 12. Slide the input in the picture to 2.8 and the target is met.

Nothing in the method asks for a whole-number answer. When the last division leaves a remainder, write the answer as a fraction or a decimal. A fraction such as 14/5 is exact, and a decimal is sometimes a rounded copy of it.

lead.text: Division is a job like any other. Write x ÷ 4 for x shared into four equal parts, and multiplying by 4 undoes it. Undo each job with its opposite, last job first.

lessons.orientation: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.
lessons.nextAction: Place a point from its coordinates and read coordinates back off a plotted point.

blocks.text: You put your socks on before your shoes. Getting undressed runs the other way: the shoes come off first, then the socks. Do it the wrong way round and the socks end up outside the shoes. Nobody has to think about it, because the order of the first job decides the order of the second.

Calculations work like that. An expression such as 2x + 3 is a short list of jobs done to a number: here, double it and then add 3. To find the number you started with, you take the jobs off again, and the order matters as much as it does with shoes.

The last lesson had equations with two moves, and the examples told you which move to make first. This lesson explains why that order works, so you can choose it yourself. It also covers an expression such as 3(x + 2), where the order is less obvious.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo a calculation one step at a time, last step first, to find the number you started with.

recap.keyIdea: To find x, undo the operations in reverse order, last one first, doing the same to both sides each time.

blocks.text: You solved 5x − 3 = 12 by adding 3 and then dividing by 5, and in 3(x + 2) = 21 you divided by the outside 3 before taking off the 2. You also found that 5x − 2 = 12 gives x = 2.8, which trying whole numbers could never have reached.

recap.nextHook: Next the numbers go onto a grid, where a pair of them pins down a single point.

lessons.title: A point is a pair

lead.text: Lay a grid over the field, with the lines one square apart and the camp at the spot where two of the lines cross. That spot is called the origin, and every walk starts there. On the map, east is to the right and north is up, so a walk has two parts: first you go across, then you go up. The squares you count on each part are the two numbers in the directions.
Mathematicians write the pair in brackets with a comma between, such as (3, 2). It reads as 3 across and 2 up. The origin itself is (0, 0), because you have walked nowhere.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the dot labelled A is at (3, 2). Count three squares to the right of the origin and then two squares up to arrive at it. Every spot on the grid has one pair, and every pair names one spot, which makes the pair an address.
That leaves one detail to settle, which is what changes when the two numbers swap places.

lead.text: Take a note that says 4 squares across and 1 up, and swap the numbers to get 1 across and 4 up. The second walk ends at a different square, a long way from the first. So the pair has to be written in a fixed order, and everyone uses the same one: across first, then up.

The two numbers have names. The first is the x-coordinate, the number of squares across. The second is the y-coordinate, the number of squares up. Together they are the coordinates of the spot. In (4, 1) the x-coordinate is 4 and the y-coordinate is 1.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows (4, 1) and (1, 4). They use the same two numbers and land on different spots. A way to remember the order is that x comes before y in the alphabet, and across comes before up.
That is enough to place a spot from its pair, which is the next job.

lead.text: Start at the origin. Do the across part of the pair first, then the up part.

reveal.text: You went across by the first number and up by the second. Swapping the numbers would have put B somewhere else.

lead.text: Your friend read the note with its numbers the wrong way round. Compare the two spots one number at a time.

reveal.text: The friend was one square out across and one square out up. Swapping the numbers moved the dig to a different square.

lead.text: So far every walk has gone right and up, but the field does not stop at the camp. There is ground to its left and below it, and the grid needs a way to say so. The answer comes from the number line. On a number line, numbers below zero sit to the left of zero, so a minus sign can mean the other way.

A negative first number means walk left instead of right. A negative second number means walk down instead of up. The point (−5, 2) is 5 squares left of the origin and 2 up. The point (3, −4) is 3 squares right and 4 down.

afterFigure.text: The sign belongs to its number and changes only the direction of that part of the walk. The size of the number still counts squares. A point with two minus signs, such as (−2, −3), is left of the camp and below it. Reaching it is still a walk across and then a walk up, with both parts going the other way.

lead.text: Here is a pair with a minus sign in it, placed one part at a time.

workedSteps.text: Start at the origin.
The x-coordinate is −4. Move 4 across, to the left.
The y-coordinate is 1. Move 1 up.
The x-coordinate is 4, so move 4 to the right.
Read the second number. What is the y-coordinate?
A y-coordinate of −2 means 2 squares down from there.

lead.text: The first number gives the position across. Keep its sign.

reveal.text: A minus sign on x means left of the origin. It stays part of the coordinate.

steps.headline: The two lines through the camp

lead.text: Two of the grid lines pass through the origin and matter more than the rest. The one that runs across is the x-axis, and the one that runs up and down is the y-axis. Each is a number line of its own, marked in squares from the origin.

A point on the x-axis has not gone up or down at all, so its y-coordinate is 0. The point (−4, 0) is one of these. A point on the y-axis has not gone across, so its x-coordinate is 0, as in (0, 3). The origin sits on both axes, which is why both of its numbers are 0.

afterFigure.text: With the axes named, you can follow any pair to its spot and read a pair back off a spot. A treasure map tests both, with a chest on the far side of the camp.

lead.text: A map puts a chest at (−2, −3), measured from camp at (0, 0). You can only walk along the grid lines: across first, then up or down.

lessons.orientation: Place a point from its coordinates and read coordinates back off a plotted point.
lessons.nextAction: Calculate a gradient from two points and say what its sign means.

blocks.text: Suppose you have buried a treasure chest in a large field and want to tell a friend where it is. “Near the big oak” is no use when the field has three oaks. You need directions that start from a place you both can find, so you pick the gate at one corner and call it the camp. The note you leave says: from the camp, walk 3 squares east and then 2 squares north.

That note uses two numbers and nothing else, and two is exactly what a flat field needs. One number fixes a spot on a single straight path, but a field has width as well as length. Maps, chess boards and the screen you are reading this on all name their places with two numbers in the same way.

The last lesson ended with numbers waiting to go on a grid. This lesson lays that grid over the field. It starts with walks across and up, and then it crosses to the far side of the camp, where the numbers need a sign.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find any spot on a grid from a pair of numbers, and write the pair for a spot you can see.

recap.keyIdea: A point is a pair (x, y), with x across and y up. A minus sign means left or down.

blocks.text: You followed a note from the camp, 3 across and 2 up, and saw that swapping the numbers sends the walk to a different square. You placed (−4, 1) by going 4 to the left and 1 up, read the y-coordinate of (4, −2) as −2, and found that the chest at (−2, −3) is a walk of 5 squares.

recap.nextHook: Join two of these points with a ruler and you have a line, and a line leans by some amount. Next you'll put a number on how steeply it leans.

lessons.title: How steep is it

lead.text: To compare the two paths, share each climb out evenly over its ground. On the short path, 30 metres of climb happens over 15 metres of ground, so each metre along brings 30 ÷ 15 = 2 metres of climb. On the winding path the same 30 metres is spread over 60 metres of ground, which gives 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 metres of climb for each metre along.

Now the comparison is easy. 2 is four times as big as 0.5, so the short path is four times as steep. The number you get by dividing the climb by the distance along the ground is called the gradient. A gradient of 2 says the path climbs 2 metres for every 1 metre you cover.
Dividing is the whole method. It works for a hill, a ramp, a roof or a line on a grid, as long as you can find the climb and the distance along.
Share the climb out evenly over the ground, as you did for the two paths.

reveal.text: You divided the climb by the distance along the ground. That quotient is the gradient. Next the same idea goes onto the grid.

steps.headline: Rise and run on the grid

lead.text: Put a path on the grid and the two measurements need new names. Pick two points on the line and move from the first to the second. The change in y is called the rise, and the change in x is called the run. They are the climb and the distance along, in grid language, so the gradient is the rise divided by the run.
In the picture the line goes from A = (1, 2) to B = (4, 5). Across the grid it moves from x = 1 to x = 4, so the run is 4 − 1 = 3. Up the grid it moves from y = 2 to y = 5, so the rise is 5 − 2 = 3.

afterFigure.text: Both are 3, so the gradient is 3 ÷ 3 = 1. The line climbs one square for every square it moves across. You do not need the picture to get these numbers. Subtracting the coordinates of the two points gives the rise and the run, and the picture only shows what the subtraction means.

lead.text: Look at the two points. The rise is how far up you go from A to B.

reveal.text: That vertical change is the rise. Divide it by the run and you have the gradient.

lead.text: The picture helps when the points are close together, but the subtraction works anywhere. To get the rise, take the second point's y-coordinate and subtract the first point's. To get the run, do the same with the x-coordinates. From (2, 3) to (5, 9) the rise is 9 − 3 = 6 and the run is 5 − 2 = 3, so the gradient is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

The order has to be the same in both subtractions. Reverse only one of them and the answer gets the wrong sign. A rise of 6 over a run of −3 would give −2, although the line really climbs. Each subtraction goes from the first point to the second, so both describe the same journey.
The next example takes a pair of points through the whole calculation, one line at a time.

workedSteps.text: Rise: subtract the y-coordinates, second minus first.
Run: subtract the x-coordinates in the same order.
Divide the rise by the run.
Rise: second y minus first y.
Run: second x minus first x.
Divide the rise by the run.

lead.text: So far every line has climbed as it moved to the right. A line can also fall. Take the points (0, 6) and (3, 0). Going from the first to the second, y drops from 6 to 0. The rise is 0 − 6 = −6 and the run is 3 − 0 = 3. That gives a gradient of −6 ÷ 3 = −2.

A negative rise means the line goes down, so the sign of the gradient tells you which way the line leans. A line that climbs as you move right has a positive gradient, and a line that falls has a negative gradient. A flat line has a rise of 0, and 0 divided by any run is 0, so its gradient is 0.

afterFigure.text: The size of the gradient, ignoring the sign, tells you how steep the line is. A gradient of 3 climbs faster than a gradient of 1/2, just as the short path climbed faster than the winding one. A gradient of −3 falls as quickly as 3 climbs.

lead.text: This line falls as it moves right. Keep the same order in both subtractions and watch the signs.

reveal.text: The rise came out negative and the run positive, so the gradient is negative, as the falling line showed.

lead.text: Not every line is steep. Keep the rise and the run apart until you divide.

lessons.orientation: Calculate a gradient from two points and say what its sign means.
lessons.nextAction: Draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and recover them from a drawn line.

blocks.text: Two points on a grid always have a straight line between them, and that line leans. Before measuring the lean on a grid, start somewhere you can feel it, which is a hillside. Say two paths lead from a car park to the same viewpoint, 30 metres higher up. One goes straight up the slope and covers 15 metres of ground on the way. The other winds gently and covers 60 metres.

Both paths climb the same height, yet the short one is far harder going. Neither number tells you how steep a path is on its own, because the steepness depends on the climb and the ground covered together.
This lesson turns that feeling into a single number. It starts with the paths and then moves the idea onto the grid from the last lesson. Lines that fall and lines that stay level come at the end.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a line's gradient from two points, and say what its sign tells you.

recap.keyIdea: The gradient is the rise divided by the run, taken in the same direction. Positive lines rise, negative lines fall and flat lines have gradient 0.

blocks.text: You compared two paths by sharing the climb over the ground, then found the gradient through (1, 2) and (3, 12) as 10 ÷ 2 = 5. The line through (−2, 3) and (2, −1) fell, so its gradient was −1.

recap.nextHook: A gradient says how steeply a line leans, but two lines with the same gradient can sit side by side at different heights. Next you'll see what fixes where a line sits, and how both numbers go into one equation.

lessons.title: From equation to line

lead.text: Light the candle and write down its height each hour. At the start it is 12 centimetres. After 1 hour it has lost 2, which leaves 10. After 2 hours it has lost 4 and stands at 8.

The pattern is that the candle loses 2 centimetres for every hour that passes. After any number of hours it has lost 2 times that number, and the height left is the starting 12 minus the loss. After 5 hours the loss is 2 × 5 = 10, so the candle stands at 12 − 10 = 2 centimetres.

Call the number of hours x and the height y, as on the grid in the last two lessons. The rule is then y = 12 − 2x. It has two numbers in it, the 12 where the candle starts and the 2 that says how fast it burns.
Use the rule from the last screen: take away what has burned from the starting height.

reveal.text: You took 3 × 2 = 6 centimetres off the 12. The next screen puts these heights on a graph.

lead.text: Now plot the heights, with the hours across and the height up. Each hour gives one point. After 1 hour the candle is at (1, 10), after 2 hours at (2, 8), and so on down to (5, 2). The grid in the picture is only 10 squares high, so the points start at the first hour, but the pattern carries on past the edge.

afterFigure.text: The points sit on a straight line. Each hour across takes the height down by 2, so the line's gradient is −2. That is the burning rate with a minus sign, because the height falls. Follow the line back to the y-axis and it crosses at 12, which is the height at the moment the candle is lit.
The height where a line crosses the y-axis is called its intercept. Two numbers fix the candle's line: the gradient says how steeply it leans, and the intercept says where it starts.

steps.headline: Writing the line as an equation

lead.text: Put the two numbers into the rule and the candle's line is y = −2x + 12. The −2 is the gradient and the 12 is the intercept. Other lines work the same way with different numbers, so the pattern is written with letters: y = mx + c. Here m stands for the gradient and c for the intercept, and each line has its own pair of values.

To see why c is the intercept, put x = 0 into the equation. The mx part becomes m × 0, which is 0, so y is just c. That puts the point (0, c) on the line, exactly where the line crosses the y-axis. For y = 3x + 4 the line crosses at height 4 and climbs 3 for every step across.
The line meets the y-axis where x is 0. Put x = 0 into the equation.

reveal.text: With x = 0 the x-term vanishes, so y is just c. That is the intercept.

steps.headline: Drawing a line from its equation

lead.text: An equation also tells you how to draw its line. Choose a value for x, replace x with it, and work out y, multiplying before you add. The pair you get is a point on the line. For y = 2x − 3, x = 0 gives y = 2 × 0 − 3 = −3, so one point is (0, −3). Choosing x = 3 gives y = 2 × 3 − 3 = 3, so another point is (3, 3).

afterFigure.text: Two points are enough, because only one straight line passes through both. Join them with a ruler and extend the line either way. You can check the result with the gradient from the two points: (3 − (−3)) ÷ 3 = 2, which is the 2 in the equation.
The substitution also works the other way. When y = 2x and y is 14, you have 2x = 14. Divide both sides by 2 and x = 7.

steps.headline: Find two points on y = 3x − 1, then draw the line.

workedSteps.text: Choose x = 0. This gives the intercept.
Choose x = 2.
Check the gradient from the two points.

steps.headline: Find the point on y = −x + 3 where x = 2.

workedSteps.text: Replace x with 2. The minus sign stays in front.
Work it out. What is y?

steps.headline: Reading the equation off a line

lead.text: Now go the other way, from a line to its equation. Say a line passes through (0, 5) and (2, 1). The point on the y-axis, (0, 5), gives the intercept at once, so c = 5. The gradient comes from the rise and the run. From (0, 5) to (2, 1) the rise is 1 − 5 = −4 and the run is 2 − 0 = 2, so m = −4 ÷ 2 = −2.

afterFigure.text: The line is y = −2x + 5. To check it, put the other point back in: when x = 2, y = −2 × 2 + 5 = 1, which matches (2, 1). A line that falls always has a negative m, as the candle's did.

lead.text: Read c from the point where x is 0. Then use both points to find the gradient.

reveal.text: The point on the y-axis gave c, and the two points gave m. Those two numbers are the whole equation.

lead.text: A container holds 2 litres and gains 0.5 litres every minute. After x minutes its volume in litres is y = 0.5x + 2. The intercept is the starting amount and the gradient is the rate.

blocks.text: A candle stands 12 centimetres tall when you light it, and it burns down by 2 centimetres every hour. If you measured it each hour and wrote the heights down, you would get 12, 10, 8, 6 and so on. A short rule holds the whole list.

The last lesson left a loose end. A gradient says how steeply a line leans, but two lines with the same gradient can sit side by side at different heights. The candle shows both halves of a line: it starts at some height, and it burns at some rate. Those two numbers are all you need to know about it.

This lesson follows the candle onto a graph, where its heights fall on a straight line. It then writes that line as an equation. The equation works for any line, so you can draw a line from it and read one back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and read both numbers back off a line.

recap.keyIdea: A line y = mx + c is fixed by two numbers: c is where it crosses the y-axis and m is its gradient.

blocks.text: You followed a candle from 12 centimetres, burning 2 an hour, to its line y = −2x + 12. Then you drew y = 3x − 1 through (0, −1) and (2, 5), and read y = 2x − 2 off the line through (0, −2) and (2, 2).

questions.prompt: Which first move keeps the solution of 2x + 6 = 18 the same?
hints: The +6 term is outside the multiplication by 2.
Choose an operation applied equally to the left and right sides.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtracting 6 from both equal sides leaves 2x = 12. Changing only one side would generally break the equality.

choices.label: Subtract 6 only from the left side
Divide only the right side by 2

questions.onCorrect: Subtract 6 from both sides. The same amount off each side keeps the balance, and 2x + 6 = 18 becomes 2x = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That changes one side only, so the two sides no longer match and the solution changes.
Dividing the right side alone leaves the left side as it was. The two sides stop being equal.

questions.prompt: Which x makes 2x = 12 true?
hints: 2x means two times x, not x plus 2.
Divide both sides of 2x = 12 by the coefficient 2.
Double your candidate and check that it returns 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing both sides by 2 gives x = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Dividing both sides by 2 undoes the × 2 and leaves x alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 12 − 2. The 2 multiplies x, so subtraction is the wrong opposite.
That is 12 × 2. 2x means 2 × x, so undo the multiplying with its opposite.

questions.prompt: Solve 4x = 20.
hints: 4x means four copies of the unknown.
Divide the total 20 into four equal parts.
Check that four times your answer equals 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing both sides by 4 gives x = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Dividing both sides by 4 undoes the × 4 and leaves x alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 20 − 4. The 4 multiplies x, so the opposite move is division.
That is 20 × 4. Multiplying makes the right side bigger. Undo a multiplication by dividing.

questions.prompt: Solve 3x − 9 = −15.
hints: Undo the subtraction of 9 first.
Adding 9 to both sides leaves 3x = −6.
Divide the negative right-hand side by positive 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding 9 gives 3x = −6; dividing by 3 gives x = −2.

questions.onCorrect: −2. Add 9 to both sides to undo the − 9, then divide both sides by 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That comes from subtracting 9. The 9 is already being taken away from 3x, so use the opposite move.
That is the value of 3x. One more move: undo the × 3 on both sides.
The sign has slipped. The right side stays negative, and a negative divided by a positive is negative.

questions.prompt: Solve 5x + 2 = 27.
hints: Remove the +2 term using the same operation on both sides.
This leaves 5x = 25.
Divide both sides by the coefficient of x, then check in the original equation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 2 gives 5x = 25; dividing by 5 gives x = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Subtract 2 from both sides, then divide both sides by 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 5x. Divide both sides by the number multiplying x.
You added 2 to the right side. The + 2 is undone by subtracting it.

questions.prompt: Why does subtracting 4 from both sides keep an equation true?

acceptedIdeas: The two sides were equal, and you took the same amount from each.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two sides were equal, and you took the same amount from each.

choices.label: The two sides were equal, and you took the same amount from each.
Subtracting always makes the numbers smaller.
It moves the 4 to the other side without changing anything.

questions.onCorrect: Equal sides with equal amounts removed are still equal.

misconceptions.feedback: Both sides do get smaller, but what matters is that each loses exactly the same amount.
Nothing moves. Each side loses 4, and that is what keeps them equal.

questions.prompt: Which route undoes “multiply by 2, then add 3”?
hints: Undo the last operation in the forward route first.
Use the inverse of addition, then the inverse of multiplication.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Undo the last operation first: subtract 3, then divide by 2. Applying inverses in the forward order would change the calculation.

questions.onCorrect: Subtract 3, then divide by 2. The last step comes off first, using its inverse.

misconceptions.feedback: That undoes the steps in the order they were done. The last step has to come off first.
The numbers are swapped. The 3 was added, so 3 is what comes off; the 2 was the multiplier.

questions.prompt: What is x?
hints: The addition of 3 happens after multiplication by 2.
Subtract 3 from both sides to leave 2x = 14.
Divide by 2, then check by multiplying and adding in the original order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 3 gives 2x = 14; dividing by 2 gives x = 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Subtracting 3 and then dividing by 2 undoes the machine in reverse order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 2x. One more step: undo the × 2.
You added 3. The + 3 is undone by subtracting 3.
You divided before taking off the 3. The last step has to come off first.

questions.prompt: Solve 3(x + 2) = 21.
hints: Here multiplication by 3 surrounds the whole bracket.
Divide both sides by 3 before changing x + 2.
Then undo the remaining addition of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing by 3 gives x + 2 = 7; subtracting 2 gives x = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The 3 multiplies the whole package, so divide by 3 first, then take off the 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x + 2. The package is still closed: take off the 2 too.
You subtracted 2 first. The 3 multiplies the whole bracket, so it comes off first.

questions.prompt: Solve x ÷ 4 − 2 = 1.5.
hints: The final operation is subtracting 2.
Add 2 to both sides to leave x / 4 = 3.5.
Undo division by 4 with multiplication by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding 2 gives x / 4 = 3.5; multiplying by 4 gives x = 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Add 2 to both sides, then multiply both sides by 4 to undo the division.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x ÷ 4. Undo the division as well, by multiplying.
You multiplied but skipped the + 2. The subtraction is the last step, so it comes off first.

hints: Work backwards through the outside operations.
Remove the outside addition, then divide by the multiplier outside the bracket.
The expression is now x − 1; undo that last subtraction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract 2, divide by 4, then add 1: x = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Take off the + 2, divide by the outside 4, then add 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x − 1. Undo the subtraction inside the brackets as well.
That is what the whole bracketed part is worth. The outside multiplier and the brackets still have to come off.

questions.prompt: Solve 4x + 1 = 4. You may enter a fraction.
hints: First remove the +1 term on both sides.
This leaves 4x = 3.
Division can give a fraction; x need not be a whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 1 gives 4x = 3; x = 3/4.

questions.onCorrect: 0.75, or 3 ÷ 4. Subtract 1, then divide by 4. An answer need not be whole.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 4x. Divide both sides by 4 to leave x alone.
You added 1. The + 1 is undone by subtracting 1.

questions.prompt: Point A is (3, 2). What is its x-coordinate?
hints: An ordered coordinate pair is written (x, y).
Read the first entry of the displayed coordinate pair.
The horizontal coordinate comes before the vertical coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate is x, so A has x = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The first number in the pair is the x-coordinate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second number, the y-coordinate. The x-coordinate comes first.

questions.prompt: Starting at the origin, which description places B = (2, 3)?
hints: Start at the origin and use the first coordinate horizontally.
Both entries in (2, 3) are positive, so use right and up.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first coordinate controls horizontal movement and the second controls vertical movement. From the origin, (2, 3) means 2 right and 3 up.

questions.onCorrect: 2 right and 3 up. The first coordinate is across, the second is up.

misconceptions.feedback: The numbers are swapped. The first coordinate is the across move.
Both numbers are positive, so neither move goes left or down.

questions.prompt: What is the x-coordinate of A = (−3, 2)?
hints: The x-coordinate is the first entry in the pair.
Keep its negative sign: it records a position left of the origin.
Read x from the displayed pair without swapping the entries.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A is three units left of the origin, so x = −3.

questions.onCorrect: −3. The minus sign stays: it means three squares to the left.

misconceptions.feedback: The minus sign is part of the coordinate. It tells you the point is left of the origin.
That is the y-coordinate. The x-coordinate is the first number.

questions.prompt: Read the second number of B = (4, −2). What is the y-coordinate?
hints: Read the second entry of the coordinate pair to find y.
Below the origin is the negative vertical direction.
Keep the minus sign when entering the second coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: B is two units below the origin, so y = −2.

questions.onCorrect: −2. The second number is y, and the minus sign means below the origin.

misconceptions.feedback: The minus sign is part of the coordinate. It tells you the point is below the origin.
That is the x-coordinate. The y-coordinate is the second number.

questions.prompt: A point is 5 units left of the origin and 1 unit up. What is its x-coordinate?
hints: Horizontal position determines x.
Moving left from the origin gives a negative coordinate.
Use the stated five-unit horizontal distance, with its direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left is negative, so x = −5.

questions.onCorrect: −5. Left of the origin is negative, so x is −5.

misconceptions.feedback: The distance is right, but left of the origin is negative. Keep the sign.
That is the move up, which is the y-coordinate. The question asks for x.

questions.prompt: A point lies on the y-axis at height 4. What is its x-coordinate?
hints: The y-axis consists of points with no horizontal displacement.
Height 4 changes y, not x.
Count the horizontal steps from the origin to the y-axis.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every point on the y-axis has x = 0.

questions.onCorrect: 0. Every point on the y-axis has no sideways move, so x is 0.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height, the y-coordinate. A point on the y-axis has not moved sideways at all.

questions.prompt: How much does y increase from A = (0, 1) to B = (2, 5)?
hints: Read the vertical coordinates of A and B.
A has y = 1 and B has y = 5.
Subtract the starting height from the ending height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The vertical change is 5 − 1 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The rise is the change in height: end y minus start y.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B's height. The increase is the change from A's height.
That adds the two heights. The increase is the difference between them.

questions.prompt: What is the gradient through (0, 1) and (2, 5)?
hints: Gradient is change in y divided by change in x.
Subtract the starting coordinate from the ending coordinate along each axis.
Divide the rise by the run in that order.
questions.onCorrect: 2. Rise ÷ run: the line goes up 2 for every 1 across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise. The rise goes on top.
That is the rise on its own. Divide it by the run.

questions.prompt: Find the gradient through (−2, 3) and (2, −1).
hints: Use the same point order in both subtractions.
Subtract the first point's y from the second point's y, and do the same for x.
A fall while moving right gives a negative gradient.
questions.onCorrect: −1. The rise is negative and the run is positive, so the line falls.

misconceptions.feedback: The line falls as it moves right, so the gradient cannot be positive.
That is the rise on its own. Divide it by the run.

questions.prompt: Find the gradient through (−2, −1) and (2, 1).
hints: Calculate the rise and run separately.
From the first point to the second, the rise is 1 − (−1) and the run is 2 − (−2).
Divide the rise by the run; a gradient can be fractional.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5, or 1 ÷ 2. A gentle line rises less than one for each step across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise. The rise goes on top.

questions.prompt: Which line rises more for each step to the right?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A gradient of 3 means a rise of 3 for each unit moved to the right. Compare that rate with the smaller positive gradients.

questions.onCorrect: A gradient of 3 rises three for each step across: more than a smaller positive gradient.

misconceptions.feedback: A gradient of 1/2 rises only half a unit per step. Compare it with the other gradient.
A horizontal line does not rise at all.

questions.prompt: A straight line goes through (1, 4) and (5, 4). Find its gradient.
hints: Both points have the same y-coordinate.
The vertical change is 4 − 4 while the horizontal change is nonzero.
Divide that vertical change by the horizontal run.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 4 − 4 = 0; dividing by the run gives gradient 0.

questions.onCorrect: 0. The rise is zero, so the line is flat.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height. The rise is the change in height, and the height stays the same.
That compares the run with itself. Work out the rise first.

questions.prompt: For y = 2x + 1, what is y when x = 0?
hints: At the vertical axis the x-term vanishes, leaving the constant term.
Multiply before adding.
The constant term is the height where x = 0.
questions.onCorrect: 1. When x is 0 the x-term vanishes, so y equals the constant: the intercept.

misconceptions.feedback: 2x means 2 × x, so it is nothing when x is 0. Multiply before you add.
Only the 2x part is zero. The constant is still there.

questions.prompt: Replace x with 2 in y = −x + 3. What is y?
hints: Substitute 2 for x while keeping the minus sign in front of x.
The expression becomes −2 + 3.
Combine the negative term with the positive constant.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Substituting x = 2 gives y = −2 + 3 = 1.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Replace x, keep the sign in front of it, then add the constant.

misconceptions.feedback: The minus sign stays with x: it is −2, not +2.
The + 3 stays positive. Combine −2 with it.

questions.prompt: Which equation matches the line through (0, −2) and (2, 2)?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The intercept is −2 because the line passes through (0, −2). Its gradient is (2 − (−2)) / (2 − 0) = 2, giving y = 2x − 2.

questions.onCorrect: The line crosses the y-axis at −2 and rises 4 over a run of 2, so m = 2 and c = −2.

misconceptions.feedback: That line falls as it goes right. This line rises.
That line crosses the y-axis above the origin. This one crosses below it.

questions.prompt: How many litres does the container hold after 4 minutes?
hints: Substitute the given x into the displayed expression.
Multiply the coefficient by the input before adding the intercept.
Add the starting amount 2 to that product.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After 4 minutes, y = 0.5 × 4 + 2 = 4 litres.

questions.onCorrect: 4 litres. Multiply the rate by the time, then add the starting amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate times the time. Add the starting amount as well.
That adds the time to the starting amount. The rate multiplies x.

questions.prompt: A line passes through (1, 2) and (3, 6). What is its gradient?
hints: Use change in y divided by change in x.
Subtract the first point's coordinates from the second point's coordinates.
Check the ratio by asking how far y rises for one horizontal unit.
questions.onCorrect: 2. Rise ÷ run: 4 up over 2 across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise. The rise goes on top.
That is the rise on its own. Divide it by the run.

questions.prompt: For the line y = 2x, which x gives y = 10?
hints: Use the stated equation y = 2x, then set y to 10.
This gives 2x = 10.
Undo multiplication by 2 and check the resulting point.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Solving 2x = 10 gives x = 5; substitution gives the point (5, 10).

questions.onCorrect: 5. Divide both sides by 2 to undo the multiplication.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 2. To undo × 2, divide both sides by 2.
That subtracts 2. The 2 multiplies x, so undo it by dividing.

questions.prompt: I'm thinking of a number. I add 5 to it and get 12. What is my number?
hints: What number, plus 5, makes 12?
Count on from 5. How many steps does it take to reach 12?
Take the 5 back off the 12 and see what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7, because 7 + 5 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 7. You worked back from 12 without writing anything down. Algebra is that thinking, written so it still works when the numbers get hard.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 12 + 5. The 5 was added to my number, so my number is smaller than 12.

questions.prompt: Which says “a number plus 5 is 12”?
hints: Read each one aloud, saying “my number” wherever you see x.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x + 5 = 12. x is the number, and + 5 = 12 says what happens to it.

questions.onCorrect: Same sentence, shorter. x is the number; the rest says what happens to it.

misconceptions.feedback: 5x means 5 × x. That's five lots of the number, not the number plus 5.
That says x is 12 + 5. Add 5 to that and you overshoot 12.

questions.prompt: Set x so the machine gives 12.
hints: Try a few values and watch what comes out.
What comes out is always 5 more than what goes in.
Which input is 5 less than the target?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With x = 7, the machine gives 7 + 5 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: x = 7 makes x + 5 equal 12. That's exactly what it means for 7 to solve x + 5 = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: With x = 17 the machine gives 22. The machine adds 5, so x has to be below 12.
12 is where the output should land. What goes in is 5 less than what comes out.

questions.prompt: The machine works out 3x − 4. If x = 6, what comes out?
hints: Start at the first box. What is 3 × 6?
Now take 4 away from that.
Multiply first, then subtract.
questions.onCorrect: 14. Multiply first, then subtract: the order is written into the expression.

misconceptions.feedback: You subtracted first. The machine multiplies first: multiplication comes before subtraction unless brackets say otherwise.
Check the first box: 3x means 3 × x, so it is 3 × 6, not 3 + 6.
That's what leaves the first box. The machine still has to subtract 4.
With x = 6, 3x means 3 × 6. It does not mean the digits 3 and 6 side by side. Multiply first, then subtract.

questions.prompt: In x + x + 4, the letter x stands for 5. Why do both x's become 5?
hints: If the two x's could differ, what would x stand for?

acceptedIdeas: Inside one expression, a letter means one number throughout.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inside one expression, a letter means one number throughout.

choices.label: Inside one expression, a letter means one number throughout.
Because 5 was the first number given.
They don't have to; one could be 3.

questions.onCorrect: One letter, one value, everywhere it appears.

misconceptions.feedback: Any value would do here. The point is that both x's get the same one.
Then x would mean two numbers at once. Within one expression it can't.

questions.prompt: Left side
hints: Start with 2 × 4.
Then add the 1.
Multiply, then add.
questions.onCorrect: 9: two lots of 4, plus 1.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 × 4 is 8. Don't forget the + 1.
2x means 2 × x, so it is 2 × 4, not 2 + 4.

questions.prompt: Is x = 4 a solution?
hints: Compare the left side you worked out with the right side.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The left side comes to 9 and the right side is 9, so the sides agree.

questions.onCorrect: Left 9, right 9. So 4 solves the equation: substituted in, the two sides agree.

questions.prompt: Is x = 3 a solution of 5x − 2 = 12? First, what is the left side when x = 3?
hints: Replace x with 3. What is 5 × 3?
Now subtract the 2.
Multiply first, then subtract, then compare with 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 × 3 − 2 = 15 − 2 = 13. 13 is not 12, so 3 is not a solution.

questions.onCorrect: 13, not 12, so 3 fails. No whole number fits, and the coming lessons find the solution without guessing.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 5 × 3. The expression then subtracts 2.
12 is the right side. Work out the left side with x = 3, then compare.
5x means 5 × x, so it is 5 × 3, not 5 + 3.

questions.prompt: What's the fare, in pounds, for a 7-mile trip?
hints: Replace m with 7.
Work out 2 × 7 first.
Then add the £3 starting charge.
questions.onCorrect: £17. The letter m let one short formula price every possible trip. That's why algebra uses letters.

misconceptions.feedback: That's (3 + 2) × 7. The £3 is paid once; only the £2 is per mile.
2m means 2 × m: two pounds for each of the 7 miles, not 2 + 7.
That's the miles part. Add the £3 starting charge.

questions.prompt: Find 3a + 2 when a = 4.
hints: Replace a with 4.
Work out 3 × 4.
Then add 2.
questions.onCorrect: 14: substitute, multiply, then add.

misconceptions.feedback: 3a means 3 × a, so it is 3 × 4, not 3 + 4.
Multiply before you add: 3 × 4 first, then + 2.

questions.prompt: Is y = 5 a solution of 2y − 3 = 7?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. 2 × 5 − 3 = 7, and the right side is 7.

questions.onCorrect: Yes: 2 × 5 − 3 is 7, the same as the right side.

questions.prompt: In n + n = 10, could the two n's be different numbers?

acceptedIdeas: No. One letter has one value, so n = 5.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. One letter has one value, so both n's are 5.

choices.label: No. One letter has one value, so n = 5.
Yes, any two numbers that add to 10.

questions.onCorrect: No: one letter, one value, so n + n = 10 means n is 5.

questions.prompt: Which x makes 3x − 4 = 14 true?
hints: Undo the final subtraction before undoing multiplication.
Add 4 to both sides of 3x − 4 = 14.
Divide the resulting right-hand side by 3.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Add 4 to both sides to undo the − 4, then divide both sides by 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 3x. Divide both sides by 3 to leave x alone.
That is 14 − 4. The − 4 is undone by adding 4.

questions.prompt: Solve x ÷ 2 + 1 = 4.
hints: Undo the outside addition of 1 first.
After subtracting 1, x / 2 must equal 3.
Multiply both sides by 2, then substitute your answer back.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 1 gives x / 2 = 3; doubling gives x = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Subtract 1, then multiply both sides by 2 to undo the division.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x ÷ 2. Undo the division as well.
You added 1. The + 1 is undone by subtracting 1.

questions.prompt: The treasure is at (3, 2), but your friend digs at (2, 3). How many single squares, each one step along a grid line, must your friend move to reach the treasure?
hints: Write down where each of you ends up: across, then up.
Compare the two places. How many squares apart are they sideways, and how many up or down?
Add the sideways gap and the up-and-down gap.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The friend is at (2, 3) and the treasure at (3, 2): one square east and one square south, so 2 moves.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The same two numbers in a different order name a different place. Order matters.

misconceptions.feedback: The numbers match, but east and north are different directions. Compare where each of you ends up.
That adds the two numbers. Count how far apart the two places are instead.
That counts only one of the two moves. The friend is out by some squares across and by some squares up.

questions.prompt: What does the minus sign in −4 tell you?

acceptedIdeas: Move left of the origin, not right.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Move left of the origin, not right.

choices.label: Move left of the origin, not right.

questions.onCorrect: A negative x means left of the origin; a negative y means below it.

misconceptions.feedback: Down is a y move. The minus sign on x changes the direction of the across move.
The order never changes. The minus sign only flips the direction of that move.

questions.prompt: A chest is buried at (−2, −3). Walking along grid lines from the camp at (0, 0), how many squares do you walk to reach it?
hints: How many squares across do you go to reach x = −2?
How many squares down do you go to reach y = −3?
Add the two walks together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 squares across and 3 squares down: 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The signs gave the directions; the sizes gave the distances.

misconceptions.feedback: The signs tell you the directions. A distance walked is never negative.
That is the difference of the two numbers. You walk both parts, one after the other.

questions.prompt: Point C is (7, −4). Swapping its two coordinates gives point D. What is the x-coordinate of D?
hints: Write D as a pair, with the coordinates in the other order.
The first number of D is the old second number.
Keep the sign of the number you move.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: D is (−4, 7), so its x-coordinate is −4.

questions.onCorrect: −4. Swapping puts the old y first, and its sign comes with it.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign travels with the number. Swapping does not make it positive.
That is C's x-coordinate. D has the numbers the other way round.

questions.prompt: A candle is 12 cm tall and burns down 2 cm every hour. How tall is it after 3 hours?
hints: How much does it burn down in 3 hours altogether?
Start from 12 and take that away.
Burn per hour times the hours, then subtract from the start.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 × 2 = 6 cm burnt, and 12 − 6 = 6 cm left.

questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. A start and a rate of change fix the whole story: that is a line.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes off one hour's burn. Count all the hours.
The candle gets shorter, not taller. Take the burn away.

questions.prompt: Why are two points enough to draw the line?

acceptedIdeas: Two points fix a straight line.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two points fix a straight line.

choices.label: Two points fix a straight line.
A line only has two points.
Only x = 0 and x = 2 are allowed.

questions.onCorrect: A straight line is fixed by any two of its points. A third point is a check.

misconceptions.feedback: A line has endless points. Two of them are enough to fix it.
Any x gives a point. Those two are just easy to work out.

questions.prompt: A line has gradient 3 and crosses the y-axis at 4. What is y when x = 2?
hints: Write its equation in the form y = mx + c.
Replace x with 2.
Multiply first, then add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line is y = 3x + 4. When x = 2, y = 3 × 2 + 4 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The line is y = 3x + 4: multiply by the gradient, then add the intercept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 3 × 2. Add the intercept as well.
That adds the three numbers. The gradient multiplies x.

questions.prompt: At what height does y = 5x + 2 cross the y-axis?
hints: The line crosses the y-axis where x is 0.
Put x = 0 into the equation.
Multiply first, then add.
questions.onCorrect: 2. At x = 0 the x-term vanishes, so the height is the constant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gradient, not the height where the line crosses.
That adds the two numbers. At x = 0, the x-term is zero.

questions.prompt: A path climbs 18 metres while you walk 6 metres along the ground. How many metres does it climb for each metre along the ground?
hints: Share the climb out evenly over the distance along the ground.
If you walk 6 metres and climb 18, what happens for just 1 metre?
Divide the climb by the distance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 metres of climb for each metre along.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Climb per step along is the idea behind gradient: how steep, in one number.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. For each metre means sharing the climb out.
That subtracts. Per metre means dividing the climb by the distance.

questions.prompt: Why do we take both differences in the same direction?

acceptedIdeas: Both changes must run from the first point to the second.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both changes must run from the first point to the second.

choices.label: Both changes must run from the first point to the second.
Because the numbers are bigger that way.
It makes no difference to the answer.

questions.onCorrect: Rise and run must follow the same journey, or the gradient comes out with the wrong sign.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of the numbers is not the reason. Both changes must describe the same journey.
It does. Reverse only one difference and the sign of the gradient flips.

questions.prompt: Find the gradient through (2, 9) and (4, 3).
hints: Take the rise first: second y minus first y.
Take the run in the same order, then divide.
The line falls as it moves right, so expect a negative answer.
questions.onCorrect: −3. The line falls three for each step to the right.

misconceptions.feedback: The line falls as it moves right, so the gradient is negative.
That is the rise on its own. Divide it by the run.

questions.prompt: What is the run from (2, 1) to (6, 9)?
hints: The run is the change in x.
Use the x-coordinates: second minus first.
6 take away 2.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The run is the change in x, from the first point to the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise, the change in y. The run is the change in x.
Take it from the first point to the second: second x minus first x.

questions.prompt: A line goes through (1, 7) and (3, 1). Is its gradient positive, negative or zero?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Negative

questions.onCorrect: Negative: y goes down as x goes up, so the rise is negative and the run is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the two heights. Does y go up or down as you move right?
The two heights differ, so the line is not flat.

questions.prompt: A bag of marbles and 3 spare marbles balance 11 marbles on the other pan. How many marbles are in the bag?
hints: Picture each pan. The bag and 3 spare marbles on one side, a heap on the other.
If you lift the 3 spare marbles off the left pan, what must you do to the right pan to stay level?
Take 3 away from the heap on the right and see what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8, because 8 + 3 = 11.

questions.onCorrect: 8. You took the spare marbles off both pans without writing anything down. That is the move this lesson names and uses.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 11 + 3. The spare marbles share a pan with the bag, so the bag holds fewer than the whole pan.
11 is the whole right pan. The left pan is the bag plus 3 spare marbles.

questions.prompt: Why divide the right side by 3 as well?

acceptedIdeas: Doing the same to both sides keeps the equation balanced.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doing the same to both sides keeps the equation balanced.

choices.label: Doing the same to both sides keeps the equation balanced.
So the right side ends up as x.

questions.onCorrect: Doing the same to both sides is what keeps the balance, whichever operation you use.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of the numbers does not matter. What matters is that both sides get the same treatment.
x ends up alone because of what the move undoes. The right side is divided to keep both sides equal.

questions.prompt: What is 2x + 8 when x = 6?
hints: Replace x with 6. What is 2 × 6?
Now add the 8.
Multiply first, then add.
questions.onCorrect: 20, the same as the right side. Putting the answer back into the original equation is the check.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 × 6. The expression then adds 8.
2x means 2 × x, so it is 2 × 6, not 2 + 6.

questions.prompt: Solve 2x − 5 = 13.
hints: Something is being taken away from 2x. Which move undoes that?
Undo the subtraction first, on both sides.
Add 5 to both sides, then divide both sides by the number multiplying x.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding 5 gives 2x = 18; dividing by 2 gives x = 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. Add 5 to both sides, then divide both sides by 2.

misconceptions.feedback: You subtracted 5. It is already being taken away, so the opposite move is needed.
That is the value of 2x. One more move: undo the × 2 on both sides.

questions.prompt: x + 2 = 9. You subtract 2 from both sides. What is the right side now?
hints: The right side started as 9.
You take 2 away from it, as you do on the left.
9 take away 2.
questions.onCorrect: 7. Whatever happens on the left happens on the right too, so the sides stay equal.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds instead of subtracting. You take the same amount off both sides.
The right side must change too. Both sides lose the same amount.

questions.prompt: Which move is the inverse of multiplying by 3?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dividing by 3

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by 3 undoes multiplying by 3, as subtracting undoes adding.

misconceptions.feedback: Subtracting undoes adding. Multiplying needs a different opposite.
That makes the number bigger in the other direction. It does not get you back to where you began.

questions.prompt: I think of a number, double it, then add 4. I get 20. What is my number?
hints: Start from the answer and work backwards.
The last thing I did was add 4. Take it off first.
Now undo the doubling: what number doubles to give what is left?
questions.onCorrect: 8. You undid the steps backwards, last step first. That is the habit this lesson builds.

misconceptions.feedback: You added 4. The last step was adding 4, so take it off.
That undoes the + 4 but not the doubling. One more step back.

questions.prompt: Why add 3 before dividing by 5?

acceptedIdeas: The − 3 was the last step, so it comes off first.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The − 3 was the last step, so it comes off first.

choices.label: The − 3 was the last step, so it comes off first.

questions.onCorrect: Undo in the reverse order: the last step in the expression is the first one off.

misconceptions.feedback: No rule puts adding first. It depends on which step was done last in the expression.
The order matters. Divide first and the − 3 would be divided too.

questions.prompt: What is 2x + 3 when x = 7?
hints: Replace x with 7. What is 2 × 7?
Now add the 3.
Multiply first, then add.
questions.onCorrect: 17, the right side of the equation. Running the machine forward checks the answer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 × 7. The expression then adds 3.
2x means 2 × x, so it is 2 × 7, not 2 + 7.

questions.prompt: In 5(x − 2), which is the last step?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The × 5

questions.onCorrect: The × 5 is last: it multiplies the whole package, so it comes off first.

misconceptions.feedback: The subtraction happens inside the brackets, which are worked out first.
You can. Brackets are worked out first, so what is outside them comes last.

flashcards.front: What must be true after substituting a solution into an equation?
flashcards.back: The left and right sides must be equal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left and right sides must be equal.

flashcards.back: Add 3 to both sides, then divide by 7: x = 3.

flashcards.front: When dividing both sides of an equation by a constant, which value is forbidden?
flashcards.back: Zero: division by zero is undefined.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero: division by zero is undefined.

flashcards.front: Which operation undoes multiplication by a nonzero number?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Division by the same number.

flashcards.front: A point is 2 units right and 4 units down from the origin. What is its y-coordinate?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The y-coordinate is −4.

flashcards.front: Which coordinate comes first in an ordered pair (x, y)?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The horizontal coordinate, x.

flashcards.front: A line rises 3 units over a run of 6 units. What is its gradient?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Gradient = 1/2.

flashcards.front: What does a negative gradient tell you as x increases?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: y decreases as x increases.

flashcards.front: For y = −2x + 5, what is the vertical intercept?
flashcards.back: At x = 0, y = 5, so the vertical intercept is 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The vertical intercept is 5.

flashcards.front: For y = 3x − 4, how much does y change when x increases by 1?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change in y is 3.

question.prompt: Solve 4x - 3 = 17. What is x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Add 3 to both sides to get 4x = 20, then divide both sides by 4: x = 5.

question.prompt: Point A is at (-4, 2). What is its x-coordinate?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An ordered pair lists x first and y second. In (-4, 2), the x-coordinate is -4.

question.prompt: What is the gradient of the straight line through A = (-2, -1) and B = (2, 7)?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 7 - (-1) = 8 and the run is 2 - (-2) = 4. The gradient is 8/4 = 2.

question.prompt: The equation is y = -2x + 6. At x = 0, what is y?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At x = 0, y = -2 × 0 + 6 = 6. This is the vertical intercept.

question.prompt: A straight line passes through A = (-3, 5) and B = (1, -3). What is its gradient?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change in y is -3 - 5 = -8 and the change in x is 1 - (-3) = 4. The gradient is -8/4 = -2.

question.prompt: A machine doubles an input and subtracts 5. What is its output for an input of 8?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output is 2 × 8 - 5 = 16 - 5 = 11.

question.prompt: Solve 5x + 4 = -11. What is x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract 4 from both sides: 5x = -15. Divide by 5: x = -3. Checking gives -15 + 4 = -11.

question.prompt: A learner turns 2x + 6 = 18 into 2x = 18. Which repair preserves equality?

acceptedIdeas: Subtract 6 from the right side too

question.prompt: Point P moves from (-2, 4) three units right and five units down. What is its new y-coordinate?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Moving down changes y from 4 to 4 - 5 = -1. The new point is (1, -1).

question.prompt: The rule is y = 3x - 2. What is y when x = -2?
The table follows one straight-line rule. What is the change in y for each increase of 1 in x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From x = 1 to x = 3, y increases by 6 while x increases by 2. The rate is 6/2 = 3 per unit of x.

question.prompt: Which equation matches every row of the table?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: y = 2x - 3. The intercept is -3 and y rises by 4 when x rises by 2, so the gradient is 2.

question.prompt: A hire service charges a fixed 9 credits plus 4 credits per hour. What does 3 hours cost? Enter the number of credits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fixed charge is added once: 9 + 4 × 3 = 21 credits.

question.prompt: Three identical packs and 4 loose tokens weigh the same as 19 tokens. Which step isolates the three packs?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Remove 4 tokens from both sides. The three packs then balance 15 tokens, so each pack contains the weight of 5 tokens.

question.prompt: An event charges 6 credits to enter and 3 credits per ride. You spend 24 credits. How many rides did you take?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Remove the fixed charge: 24 - 6 = 18 credits. Divide by the cost per ride: 18/3 = 6 rides.

question.prompt: On a map, a marker starts at (3, -2). It moves 5 units west and 4 units north. What is its final x-coordinate?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: West decreases x: 3 - 5 = -2. North changes y, so the final point is (-2, 2).

question.prompt: A tank empties at a constant rate. Using the table, what is the signed change in litres per minute?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The volume changes by 16 - 28 = -12 litres over 6 - 2 = 4 minutes. The signed rate is -12/4 = -3 litres per minute.

question.prompt: A machine adds 4 units of length per minute. After 3 minutes, the length is 19 units. What was the length at time zero?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Use length = 4 × time + starting length. Substituting gives 19 = 4 × 3 + starting length, so the starting length is 7 units.
